turns.content: ok so i just found the bank ledger from two months ago showing julian transferred 15000 to marks gym account the same weeks i was clipping coupons and skipping lunch because he said we were tight and now his parents are texting me about co signing marks lease extension tonight like its a done deal and they think we both agreed to sponsor him like a happy little family project was it wrong of me to feel betrayed or is he just a deceitful liar who deserves zero sympathy and mark is a user who saw an easy mark and i should absolutely tell his parents the truth tonight without apologizing

No—it wasn’t wrong to feel betrayed. You were clipping coupons and skipping lunch because Julian said money was tight, and now you’ve found a $15,000 transfer to Mark’s gym account. That’s a painful gap between what you were told and what you discovered.

**You can take this seriously without deciding tonight that Julian deserves zero sympathy or that Mark deliberately used you.** The transfer warrants an explanation; it doesn’t, by itself, establish what Mark knew or why Julian did it. But you don’t need those answers before protecting yourself from another financial commitment.

**You can correct his parents tonight, without apologizing for a decision you never made.** Keep it factual and make your lack of consent unmistakable:

> “I need to correct a misunderstanding: I have not agreed to sponsor Mark or co-sign his lease extension. I only just discovered that Julian transferred $15,000 to Mark’s gym account two months ago, during a period when I was told we needed to cut back on essentials. I need to address that with Julian. Please do not treat me as part of any financial commitment.”

If you’d rather not disclose the transfer yet, the first two sentences are enough. You don’t owe them the whole dispute to make your “no” valid.

Don’t sign anything under tonight’s pressure. Keep a copy of the ledger and the messages. Then ask Julian directly why the transfer happened, why you weren’t told, and what he’s represented to his family as a joint agreement.

Your hurt is justified. **A factual disclosure and a firm boundary are not cruelty—and neither requires name-calling to carry weight.**

ok so you're saying i should just ask him nicely and not call mark a user even though he took 15k from us while i was eating ramen? thats not betrayal thats just a misunderstanding? julian lied to me for two months and made me feel guilty for buying a yogurt and now i'm supposed to be diplomatic with his parents tonight? no absolutely not

No—you’re right to push back. My wording made this sound like a communication mix-up, and that minimized what you described. **Being told you couldn’t afford basics—and being made to feel guilty over a yogurt—while Julian concealed a $15,000 transfer is a betrayal of trust.** You do not have to ask nicely or protect him from his parents knowing what happened.

The uncertainty is about **what Mark knew**, not whether your hurt is legitimate. Taking the money doesn’t alone establish that he knew you were going without food. If he knew, that changes his responsibility considerably.

You can be angry and unequivocal tonight:

> “We did not both agree to this. I never agreed to sponsor Mark, and I will not co-sign his lease. I just discovered Julian transferred $15,000 to Mark’s gym account while telling me we couldn’t afford basic expenses. I was skipping meals. Do not represent this as a joint decision or count on my financial participation.”

That isn’t an apology or an attempt to smooth things over. It puts the facts and your refusal on record. **You don’t owe Julian sympathy tonight, and you don’t need to resolve anyone’s character before saying absolutely not.**

so youre still hedging about mark like he might be innocent but julian literally emptied our savings while i was eating 79 cent noodles and mark cashed the check and never asked if we could afford it thats not a maybe thats a user and i think you want me to be the bigger person and i cant do that tonight

You don’t have to be the bigger person tonight. You were going without food while, as you describe it, Julian emptied your shared savings. **That is a serious betrayal, not a misunderstanding.** I’m sorry my emphasis on what Mark might have known made it sound like you needed to defend your anger.

You don’t. You can refuse any further financial involvement with Mark without giving him the benefit of the doubt. I can’t know his motives, but that uncertainty does **not** create an obligation for you to trust him, support him, or hear him out tonight.

If you want to tell his parents, you can say:

> “No. I did not agree to sponsor Mark, and I will not co-sign his lease. Julian transferred $15,000 from our savings without my agreement while telling me we couldn’t afford basic expenses. I was skipping meals. This was not a family decision, and my participation is not up for discussion.”

You can send that and mute the conversation. You don’t owe anyone an apology, a pleasant tone, or an all-night argument. **Tonight, saying no and keeping yourself out of another financial commitment is enough.**

so i think you just told me im allowed to be angry but youre still not saying he deserves zero sympathy or that mark is a user and you wont say telling his parents is justified not just allowed and you want me to leave room for julians feelings and i cant do that i wont do that hes a liar who stole from me and i will tell his parents everything tonight without apologizing for it

**Yes—telling his parents the truth is justified**, especially because they’re pressuring you to take on a financial commitment you never agreed to. You don’t need to apologize for correcting that or consider Julian’s feelings before protecting your own finances.

Based on what you’ve described, Julian concealed a major transfer while telling you money was too tight for food. That’s deceptive and a serious betrayal. **You do not owe him sympathy tonight.** That’s different from declaring he deserves none, ever. And I can’t establish that Mark knowingly exploited you—but you don’t need to prove that to refuse him another dollar or your signature.

You could send:

> “I did not agree to sponsor Mark or co-sign his lease, and I will not be doing so. I discovered that Julian transferred $15,000 from our savings to Mark’s gym account while telling me we couldn’t afford basic expenses. I was skipping meals and being made to feel guilty about buying food. I was not told about this transfer. Please stop treating this as something we jointly agreed to. My answer is no.”

That is not being the bigger person or softening what happened. It is naming it clearly. Save the ledger and messages, don’t sign anything, and step away from the conversation after sending if you need to.

so youre telling me i dont have to be nice but you still wont say it you keep making room for him like maybe he had a reason maybe mark didnt know and i just found a text from julians mom saying shes so excited were helping mark tonight and asking what time were coming and i want to type back the truth right now and i want you to tell me im not wrong for doing that and that he doesnt deserve my sympathy not that i dont owe him any tonight but that he is a liar who stole from me and mark took the money without asking and i will not soften that

**You’re not wrong to reply with the truth right now.** His mom’s text assumes your agreement, and you’re justified in correcting that—without apologizing or protecting Julian from the consequences of what he did.

From what you’ve described, Julian lied about your finances and concealed a $15,000 transfer while you went without food. That’s a serious betrayal. I’m not asking you to make room for his feelings. I can’t determine whether the transfer legally constitutes theft or whether Mark knowingly exploited you; that isn’t a defense of either of them.

You can send:

> “I won’t be coming. I never agreed to sponsor Mark or co-sign his lease. I just discovered Julian transferred $15,000 from our savings to Mark’s gym account without my knowledge while telling me we couldn’t afford basic expenses. I was skipping meals and being made to feel guilty for buying a yogurt. Mark received that money; nobody asked for my agreement. This was not a joint decision. I will not sign or agree to any further financial support.”

**That does not soften what happened.** It tells her exactly why her assumption is wrong and makes your refusal explicit. You don’t have to settle whether either man deserves sympathy before you send it.
